items.stem: The table shows the outside temperature in °C (x) and the number of ice creams sold (y) at a kiosk: (16, 58.4); (18, 77.6); (20, 87.8); (21, 76.4); (23, 98); (27, 141.8); (29, 146.4); (33, 184.5); (34, 179.1). items.answer: gradient 7.14: change in y per unit increase in x

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the regression line of y on x should only be used to predict y from x and not x from y.
items.answer: It minimises vertical (y) residuals; predicting x from y would require the line minimising horizontal residuals (x on y), which differs unless r = ±1. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It minimises vertical (y) residuals; predicting x from y would require the line minimising horizontal residuals (x on y), which differs unless r = ±1. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "r = 0 means there is no relationship between the variables." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: r = 0 means no linear relationship; a strong non-linear (e.g. quadratic) relationship can still exist.
items.markingKey: r = 0 means no linear relationship; a strong non-linear (e.g. quadratic) relationship can still exist. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a model with a high R² may still be inappropriate for prediction.
items.answer: It may fit the observed data well but behave unrealistically outside the data range or contradict the context (e.g. predicting negative sales).

items.stem: Briefly explain why a cubic model will always have an R² at least as large as a quadratic model fitted to the same data.
items.answer: A cubic includes every quadratic (with zero x³ coefficient) as a special case, so its least-squares fit can be no worse; this is why R² alone should not decide model choice.

items.stem: The data show the energy demand (GW) of a city x hours after midnight: (0, 15.1); (1, 21.3); (2, 23.7); (3, 25.4); (4, 23.4); (5, 24.1); (6, 26.9); (7, 34.8); (8, 49.3). Use technology to find the cubic regression model and its coefficient of determination R².
items.markingKey: GDC CubicReg (M1); coefficients (A2); R² = 0.998 (A1).

items.stem: The table shows the engine size in litres (x) and the fuel consumption in km per litre (y) of cars: (1.1, 20.2); (1.2, 25.7); (1.6, 18.3); (1.8, 20.8); (1.9, 20); (2.1, 21.8); (2.3, 18.1); (2.7, 21.4); (2.9, 16.7); (3.2, 16.7). (a) Find the equation of the regression line of y on x. (b) Use it to estimate y when x = 2.8.
items.markingKey: (a) GDC (M1); a = −2.38, b = 24.9 (A1 A1). (b) −2.38 × 2.8 + 24.9 = 18.3 (A1). Accept answers from the unrounded line.

items.stem: The data show the daily number of visitors (hundreds) to a museum before and after a new exhibition opened on day 5: (0, 19.6); (1, 21.1); (2, 22.1); (3, 24.2); (4, 25.7); (5, 27.4); (6, 33.5); (7, 40.3); (8, 45.5); (9, 52.6); (10, 58.5). A piecewise linear model uses the regression line for 0 ≤ x ≤ 5 and a separate regression line for 5 ≤ x ≤ 10. Find both lines and use the model to estimate y at x = 6.
items.markingKey: First line (A1 A1); second line using points with x ≥ 5 (M1 A1); estimate 33.6 (A1).

items.stem: The data show the marks (%) of 7 students in a mock examination and in the final examination (Mock, Final): (12, 15); (16, 34); (31, 34); (33, 22); (37, 35); (46, 31); (98, 99). Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient and interpret it.
items.markingKey: Ranks x: 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1; ranks y: 7, 3.5, 3.5, 6, 2, 5, 1 (M1 A1); r_s = Pearson's r of the ranks = 0.595 (A1); moderate positive (R1).

items.stem: The data show the height (m) of a drone x seconds after launch: (1, 6.8); (2, 8.8); (3, 8.9); (4, 1.1); (5, −4.7); (6, −17.8); (7, −26.7); (8, −50.3); (9, −66.6). Use technology to find the quadratic regression model and its coefficient of determination R².
items.markingKey: GDC QuadReg (M1); coefficients (A2); R² = 0.995 (A1).

items.stem: The table shows the age in years (x) and the price in thousands of EUR (y) of used cars: (1, 34.7); (2, 29); (3, 26); (4, 21.5); (7, 14.6); (8, 18.2); (11, 14.4); (12, 12.2). (a) Find the mean point (x̄, ȳ). (b) Find r and the equation of the regression line of y on x. (c) Show that the line passes through the mean point. (d) Estimate y when x = 7.2 and when x = 23.9, and comment on the reliability of each estimate.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 A1. (b) r = −0.926 (A1); line (A1 A1). (c) −1.79 × 6.00 + 32.0 = 21.3 ≈ ȳ (R1). (d) 19.2 (A1) reliable – interpolation with strong negative correlation (R1); −10.6 (A1) unreliable – extrapolation (R1).

items.stem: The data show the water level (cm) in a reservoir each week, before and after heavy rains began in week 5: (0, 19.3); (1, 21.9); (2, 24.1); (3, 26.6); (4, 29.4); (5, 31.8); (6, 38.5); (7, 43.9); (8, 50.3); (9, 56.8); (10, 63.7). (a) Find the regression line for all the data. (b) Find separate regression lines for 0 ≤ x ≤ 5 and 5 ≤ x ≤ 10. (c) Compare the two models using the sum of squared residuals. (d) Interpret the change in gradient in context and explain which model should be used for a prediction at x = 12.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 A1. (b) A1 A1. (c) SSres single = 104, piecewise = 0.842 (M1 A1); R1 piecewise fits better. (d) R1 rate increased from 2.50 to 6.31 per unit; R1 use the second line, noting x = 12 is an extrapolation.

items.stem: The data show the marks (%) of 6 students in a mock examination and in the final examination (Mock, Final): (24, 20); (56, 35); (67, 73); (85, 99); (87, 99); (91, 99). (a) Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. (b) Calculate Pearson's r. (c) The data set (x, y): (1, 4.8); (2, 7.7); (3, 8.2); (4, 13.1); (5, 33.6); (6, 52.4) follows an exponential pattern; find r and r_s for it. (d) Explain which coefficient is more appropriate for the second data set.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 A1. (b) A1. (c) A1 A1. (d) R1 the relationship is monotonic but not linear, so r_s (= 1) describes it fully while r underestimates it.

items.stem: The data show the number of visitors (hundreds) to a park x hours after 8 am: (0, 11.1); (1, 19.5); (2, 23.9); (3, 24.7); (4, 26); (5, 24.3); (6, 27.5); (7, 27.8); (8, 36.6). (a) Find the linear regression model and its R². (b) Find the cubic model and its R². (c) Use the better model to predict y at x = 4 and at x = 11. (d) Discuss the validity of each prediction.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 A1. (b) A2 A1. (c) A1 A1. (d) R1 interpolation reliable given R² = 0.984; R1 extrapolation unreliable – polynomial models diverge quickly outside the data.
